title: The Body
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reflects on the challenges and problems of life, acknowledging that even in peaceful settings, difficulties can arise, but also encourages the audience to look beyond their immediate experiences and consider the broader context of suffering and injustice, such as the threat of a wildfire or the legacy of slavery and oppression. He invites the audience to cultivate awareness and compassion for themselves and others, and to approach life with a sense of hope and resilience. By doing so, we can find a deeper understanding of ourselves and our place in the world, and develop a more nuanced and compassionate response to the complexities of life.

sentences.text: Good morning again, everybody.
Here we are on the eighth day of our seven-day sesshin.
I guess we're all almost ready to stop on to other things, but we probably could go on just this way for a while.
Sesshin really is the perfect life.
Everything is taken care of, nothing extra.
All we have to do is breathe, walk up and down, eat, clean up a little bit, stand, lie down, see, hear, smell, taste, touch, think, enjoy our life.
No problems.
So now that we're almost done, we're going to get ready to resume our many problems.
Life is problems, right?
That's the first truth of Buddha.
Life is problems.
The world is really marvelous.
The way it goes this way, and then it goes that way, and then it comes back again this way, and then it goes that way again.
Nobody's in charge.
Nobody gets to have it their way.
Nobody knows what's going on.
But we do know that good is good, and we are trying.
Speaking of problems that go this way and then they go that way, possibly some of you have heard that there are once again, as we're now always expecting, big fires in California.
One of them is in the Los Padres National Forest in the Ventana Wilderness, exactly where Tassajara is.
And I know many of you know Robin, she was down there at Tassajara, and they had to evacuate the small crew of people that were there.
So I don't know how many times it's been that Tassajara was seriously threatened by fire, and here we are again, so early in the season.
Usually it's late summer, fall.
So this morning I heard from Rinchen Bunce, who sent me this report from the newspaper.
Winds out of the west are pushing the fire toward Tassajara Zen Center, a monastery and retreat center in a remote mountain valley in the Ventana Wilderness.
The center provided an update on the fire status Saturday, today, on its website, and this is from the newspaper telling us what it says on the Zen Center website.
There was moderate fire activity last night, and the fire has moved closer to Tassajara.
A crew of 10 firefighters worked with the Tassajara fire crew yesterday and through the night helping with fire prep and cutting fire lines.
Dharma rain was run until 11 p.m.
The area is damp and the water supply is good.
Dharma rain is the system that they installed a few years ago to wet everything, so that theoretically even if the fire is all around there, everything is wet, and so the fire won't spread there.
It will go somewhere where it's friendlier to the fire.
So we have very good reason to hope that even though this is you know very bad, as it always is, that Tassajara will be spared.
But of course you never know.
So there's always a reason to be concerned and good reason to offer prayers and chanting for Tassajara.
Today is Juneteenth.
We've noticed this before when it was June 19th on sesshin, but this year for the first time it is a national holiday, officially a national holiday.
The government has so declared.
June 19th 1865 the army marched into Galveston, Texas and told the people there who had been thinking that they were still enslaved, that they were no longer enslaved.
Can you imagine hearing this?
When you had no idea of it, the joy you would feel.
I think we don't know the history of the suffering of this world in the past.
We don't really know the history.
We know that there's always been social suffering, but history is always written by the underwritten, so to speak, paid for by the people who are in charge of things.
So it's always the history of the great men and the women and all their notable doings.
What we call history, like what we call news, is not what goes on.
It's obvious, right?
But yet somehow we're seduced into thinking, oh this is what happened today.
I read it in the news.
This is what happened before.
I read it in the history.

Well now we are learning that among the great sufferings of this world throughout history it's very possible that the suffering caused by the institution of black slavery in the United States, its length of time, how long it went on, its brutality, and its just fundamental wrongness.
And the fact that even after it was over it persisted for so long, even to the present, this surely must be one of the worst instances of suffering and injustice of all time.
And it's a wound right in the middle of our hearts, a wound that has never been sufficiently acknowledged, much less healed.
So that's why it's so good and so inspiring that now we have actually a day, however mixed up its origins are, that commemorates and celebrates the end of slavery here.
A great occasion for joy.
So happy Juneteenth everybody.
And you know we'll be able this afternoon to have fun and celebrate Juneteenth.
And I hope that you have a chance to do that with the happy glow of sesshin still surrounding your body, but also that you will think about what this day means and what it means to you.
And since we're acknowledging commemorations and special days, we have another one coming tomorrow.
It's Father's Day tomorrow, so let me be the first to wish all of you who are fathers happy Father's Day.
All of us have or have had fathers and I hope that tomorrow will be a day of honoring them, although as we all know fathers don't always do such a great job.
I will confess to you that I myself have not done such a great job.
Maybe I've been thinking of other things besides being a father, but even so it's a good thing to honor our fathers.
It's good for us, it's good for them too.

This week in the talks that I've been giving I've been emphasizing the body alive, dead, the breath in the body, throughout the body, the body as the fundamental basis of our practice, of our suffering, of our human life.
Currently in the language that they use black activists talk about black bodies.

My friend Rhonda McGee who's one of the leading spokespersons for mindfulness in contemplating racism often uses the phrase black bodies, and I always feel a little confused when I hear this and I'm not so sure what it means.
It doesn't sound so good to me, black bodies.

I guess it refers to the way black people in our world have been objectified, seen as literally just stuff that could be bought and sold, and how because black people are usually so physically identifiable as black people they can be targeted, they can be excluded, they can be diminished, and they can literally be as harmed as we've been so painfully aware of how the police can target black bodies, like they say, and I'm sure that our collective guilt which is probably much buried in us over the oppression of black people all this time has led white people to have an irrational fear and dread of black bodies.
So the idea of black bodies to me is a terrible and a painful reminder of what has happened, but it's a reduction of what black people or any of us are.
We're not stuff.
We're not bodies.
We're Buddhas.
We're sacred presences.
Maybe you noticed this in what I read for you yesterday from Zhenju Earthland-Manuel writing about the Zen mirror practice of Tokeiji.

Sit long enough with the body in all its detail, and you pass through the body to the other side, beyond black, white, male, female, and as we've been contemplating all week, we are the body, and the body is more than the body.
The body is the breath.
The body is profound peace.
The body is the flow of all life.
Everything is right here in this body.

All beings, all consciousness, this profound rhythm of living and dying, of being and not being, all of it is expressed in this body that we've been sitting with all week long, and I know that we've all felt this, maybe just for a moment, maybe for whole days at a time during sesshin.
In the Tokeiji mirror practice that both Zhenju and Ruth Ozeki were practicing, both of them wrote about looking in the mirror and seeing the aging face.
In Zhenju's piece, she says that in the end, being old, like being black, isn't anything.
We have feelings about it.
Soon they pass.
And yeah, maybe we're old.
Let's not deny it.
Maybe we're black.
We can't escape it.
But also, as she writes, in the silence, we aren't anymore.
That, or rather by being that, we go beyond it.
It reminded me of a poem of mine about being old, which I wrote when I thought I was old, but I wasn't too old then.
Now I'm older than ever.
Do you know that?
Today I'm older now than I've ever been.
So this is a poem about this that is from the opening sequence of poems in my book, I Was Blown Back, which is a pretty good book, actually.
I recommend it.
Hardly anybody read it, I think.
But anyway, here's the poem.

*Being old isn't the bodily sensations are pleasant, unpleasant, interpreted in reference to memory, obey the social construct of age, agreement, designation, imputed on reading a face in the mirror, which with advancing time, in reference to a fixture in the soul of self's melodious repetition, is an object of questioning, searching, look in eyes, brightness, shins, slump.
All ages persist as one always.
There's nor old nor young but additions in the inventory of resignations in the fact of the face, or as the face, the silence in what comes and goes in and out the opening.*
I'll just read that one more time.

*Being old isn't the bodily sensations are pleasant, unpleasant, interpreted in reference to memory, obey the social construct of age, agreement, designation, imputed on reading a face in the mirror, which with advancing time, in reference to a fixture in the soul of self's melodious repetition, is an object of questioning, searching, look in eyes, brightness, shins, slump.
All ages persist as one always.
There's nor old nor young but additions in the inventory of resignations in the fact of the face, or as the face, in the silence in what comes and goes in and out the opening.*
While I'm quoting myself, I'll share with you some of the few paragraphs from an essay in When You Greet Me, I Bow called What is the Body?
So here's a little bit from that.
We think about our bodies all the time.
How do they look?
What is their state of health?
Are they aging?
Are they sufficiently strong, attractive, impressive?
These questions churn out an almost endless stream of thinking, feeling, and spending.
Consider all the clothing, beauty products, food products, accessories, books, equipment, therapists, health products, body workers, and so on, that make up such a huge portion of our economy.
Thank God for the obsession of the body.
You would not have an economy without it.
Everything does depend on the body.
Without it, we are literally nothing.
Transcendent concepts such as consciousness, soul, higher self, Buddha nature, is there any such thing?
If there were, wouldn't all these things also depend on the body?
But what is the body?
We take it totally for granted.
Just like we take for granted the sky and the earth.
Just like the sky and the earth, the body is much more than we know.
What we think of as our body, what we feel, imagine, and dream about, what we unthinkingly assume it to be, is not really what the body is.
And what self is there that's not the body?
And yet, where is that self that possesses a body to call its own?
Who outside the body utters the words, my body?
Without a tongue, without a brain, I can't even utter those words.
So ask yourself, from what perspective are you looking at your body?
From inside, peering out from body's eyes, or from outside, as if you're looking at a portrait in a portrait gallery?
How could the body be external to itself?
No, that can't be.
The body must be contained in the experience of looking.
So what you see and call my body has got to be something else.
Is it the flow of sensory experiences—seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, tactile sensation?
But no, that's also a problem.
Because where is smelling and tasting?
Is it in the nose?
The tongue?
Is it in the tongue?
Is it in the stuff that you're smelling and tasting?
Is it in the brain?
Where is it?
And then there's this question of awareness, the insubstantial, apparently non-physical process through which anything we experience comes to us.
Is awareness inside the body or outside?
If it was inside, we could never have an idea of my body.
That would be absurd.
There would be no one outside who could say mine.
But if awareness is outside the body, that's impossible, right?
We know that's not right.
Yet awareness is foundational to experiencing oneself as a person at all.
Without awareness, there's no smelling, no tasting, no body.
You could have flesh without awareness, but that would not be a living human body.
A living human body is aware of being a body.
In the avidharma, the Buddhist analysis of experience, there's no body.
There's just various categories of momentary mental events.
Some of them we categorize as physical, but they're not really physical.

If I say I have an ache in my right leg or a pain in my lower back, like I had this morning, the avidharma analysis says that this sensation is a mental event produced in consciousness when an object that I call my lower back activates inner sensors that awaken awareness in a particular way.
Likewise, seeing, hearing, and all sense perceptions are mental events stimulated by apparently physical objects called rupa.
So in the Buddhist analysis, there's no body.
There's rupa, as I said, which is some kind of illusory arising that appears to be solid and that forms a basis for experience that we call physical.
But in actual fact, there's not something there.
There's just a continuous flow of momentary conscious events of different sorts.

The early Buddhist practitioners were analyzing their experience in that way with the help of their meditation practice, so they could disabuse themselves of attachment to their bodies because there was nothing there actually to attach to.
There was just the flow of experiences.
But let's be honest, we are very convinced we have bodies.
Beyond our misinterpretation of our personal experiences, the idea of the body is reinforced by social discourse.
The idea of the body is reinforced by social discourse.
That's one of the main insights of contemporary thinking about the African American experience, that it's socially determined.
Being Black is socially determined.
It's not something inside of somebody.
So we all have bodies that are not bodies, but they're determined by people around us who define us in certain ways.
Then we all come away believing we have bodies.
Our whole system of language, in fact, is based on the metaphor of the body.
Most of our feelings and most of the things we think about our lives are based on the metaphor of the body.
A thought so foundational to us, we can't even begin to know how to question it.
It's interesting to think about the story of the Buddha's awakening.
Remember, on the night of the Buddha's awakening, according to the story, he is visited by the forces of Mara as trying to stop the Buddha from awakening.
Most of Mara's devastating and spectacular displays of hopes and fears had to do with the body.
Some of them were temptations and sensual allurements.
Some of them were threats to harm, and Mara said, "This is my army.
Where's your army, Buddha?"
And remember what the Buddha did?
He touched the earth, and he said, "Here's my army.
Here's my support."
In touching the earth, Buddha was not just calling on the earth goddess to be his protector.
He was saying, "My body is the earth.
The earth is my body.
My body is an expression of earth.
It is produced and supported by earth.
It is made entirely of elements of earth, and there's nothing on earth, no matter how frightening, that can threaten this indestructible earth body."
Even if it's broken up into a million gazillion pieces, as it will be one day, it remains.
It goes home to its mother who gave birth to it, who embraces it now as I'm sitting here, Mara, and always will embrace it so I have absolutely nothing to fear.
And in Mahayana Buddhism, the body of the Buddha is further elaborated.

Now the Buddha has three bodies: the dharmakaya body, the truth body, which is measureless, all-encompassing, perfect, beyond perception and concept; the sambhogakaya body, the enjoyment body, purified, perceived body of perfect meditation and teaching, the body of the sutras, the body of all the Buddha images we see and have on our altars; and then there's the nirmanakaya, the transient historical body that appears in our world for the purpose of teaching beings in this world.
In our Zen teachings, it's axiomatic that the ordinary human body that can be accessed in meditation practice is itself, as I said before, beyond the body as we normally conceive of it.
Dogen calls it the true body.
He says the true body is far beyond the world's dusts.
He says, I think, in *Fukanzazengi* that we probably chanted this week, or as Hakuen Zenji puts it in the *Song of Zazen*, "this very body is the body of Buddha."
But the actual biological, physiological human body actually is really marvelous.
It's an endlessly complex occurrence.
Three hundred years of intense medical science has told us a lot, but still it's only scratched the surface.
That's why Leah's still getting grants and still studying the body, because it's like, we almost know nothing.
There's so much more to know.
I mean, just take the brain.
How could that brain, how does it work?
Nobody has any idea how it regulates everything instantaneously, adjusting to all kinds of contingencies, producing thoughts.
How does a brain produce a thought?
Producing thoughts, literary works, skyscrapers, giant cities, social systems, and so on.
How does the heart work?
How does the lungs work?
Cells, DNA, RNA, the enormous knowledge and complex communication and movement that seem to occur effortlessly within every human body.
As without even thinking about it, we walk, we run, we jump, we shout, we sing, we sit down and play the piano.
How does that happen?
Twenty-five thousand miles, I always say this, I still can't believe it, twenty-five thousand miles of blood vessels in the human body.
Stretched out, it goes around the world, literally, and blood is always moving in those twenty-five thousand miles of blood vessels, nurturing every single cell in the body.
Unbelievable, this human body.
It is a marvel, and nobody designed it, and nobody manufactured it.
There's no patents for the body.
No one knows how all this happened, really.
And the consciousness associated with the body, the consciousness that knows itself, nobody knows anything about that.
And as we've been saying in our practice, we really honor the body and we practice with the body.
It's really about our body.
We're paying attention, as we've been saying all week, to the details of our body.

And not only when we sit, I mean, when we first get instruction in zazen, they say, you know, stand this way, walk this way, bow to your cushion, bow away from your cushion, sit down this way, here's how you walk and kinhin, and so on.
It's very, it's very, very physical.
And this is what we're practicing with, not some spiritual insight, some teaching we're going over and thinking about while we're sitting, just the body.
One of the deepest themes in Western philosophy, beginning with Plato, is the idea that the world of appearances in which things come and go is not real.
And so the job of the intellect, the job of the spirit, is to carry us beyond this corrupt physical world to a perfected world of non-material form that is purely mental or spiritual.
And that was always the task of religion and philosophy in Western thought.

Up until the twentieth century, when phenomenology, which I think perhaps in some part anyway was under the influence of Buddhism, which never had a mind-body split, phenomenology began to break this Western task down.

In our Earth-threatened time, when the physical planet Earth that we live on has been challenged by our activity, it makes sense that we're now ready to begin to learn and enact the truth that has always been engraved on our very skins, that mind, body, spirit, and Earth are one expression, one concern, and one delight.
So I want to conclude now with another poem.
This one is by the great poet Robert Creeley, and I was talking to Bob Rose yesterday, and Rose yesterday, and Bob told me about this poem, which I either forgot or never knew.
Bob Creeley was the greatest poet.
I love Bob Creeley's poem.
I can't even explain to you how much his work has meant to me over all these years I've been reading him since the mid-1960s.
Sometimes I have to stop reading him for long periods of time because he's too good.
It just drives me crazy.
I start writing like Robert Creeley, and it's hopeless.
Anyway, I know a lot of people, including Bob Rose, who knew Bob Creeley.
I didn't really know him.
I met him once or twice.
I wish I knew him.
Anyway, here's his poem.
*The plan is the body.
The plan is the body.
There is each moment a pattern.
There is each time something for everyone.
The plan is the body.
The mind is in the head.
It's a moment in time, an instant, a second.
The rhythm of one, and one, and one, and one.
The two, the three.
The plan is in the body.
Hold it an instant.
In the mind, hold it.
Hold it.
What was said, you said.
The two, the three.
Times in the body.
Hands, feet, you remember.
I, I remember.
I, speak it, speak it.
The plan is in the body.
Times you didn't want to, times you can't think, you want to.
You, me, me, remember.
Me, here.
Me, wants to.
Me, am, thinking of you.
The plan is the body.
The plan is the body.
The sky is the sky.
The mother, the father.
The plan is the body.
Who can read it?
Plan is the body.
The mind is the plan.
I, speaking.
Memory gathers like memory.
Plan, I thought to remember, thinking again, thinking.
The mind is the plan of the mind.
The plan is the body.
The plan is the body.
The plan is the body.
The plan is the body.*
Isn't that a great poem?

So, anyway, I'm finished and I want to just finally thank you all again for your practice, for your contributions to the Sangha, all of you, all the chanting and the bell ringing and the planning and the beautiful altars on our screens and the announcements and the Dharma talks and the sitting and the walking, everything.
Thank you so much for your practice, for your contributions to the Sangha and to the world.
Everything is always confusion.
Everything is always going to pot.
No matter what year it is in history, people are sitting around and talking about how everything is going to pot and something has to be done.
And we're always trying to figure out what are we going to do about all this?
And we have to do something.
Every one of us has something that we really have to do and we will do it.
And practice is so important.
Practice so much helps us.
And supporting and upholding practice is one of the things that we have to do.
So thank all of you very, very much for doing that.
I'm quite inspired by it and I look forward to the next time we will see each other again.
So that's my talk and let's chant and then we'll see what we do next.
